message.content:
**The “Three Great Schisms” of Christianity** | # | Schism | Approximate dates | Key causes & figures | Main outcome | |---|--------|-------------------|----------------------|--------------| | 1 | **The Great Schism (East–West Schism)** | 1054 – c. 1100 | • Long‑standing theological, liturgical, and political differences between the Latin West and Greek East.
• Disputes over the *Filioque* clause, papal primacy, and the use of unleavened bread.
• The mutual excommunications of Patriarch Michael I Cerularius (Constantinople) and Pope Leo IX. | Formal split into the Roman Catholic Church (West) and the Eastern Orthodox Church (East). The schism remains today, though there have been numerous attempts at dialogue and reconciliation. | | 2 | **The Protestant Reformation** | 1517 – 1648 | • Martin Luther’s 95 Theses (1517) criticized indulgences and other church practices.
• Spread of reform ideas by Huldrych Zwingli, John Calvin, and others.
• Political support from princes and city‑states, and the invention of the printing press. | Creation of a wide array of Protestant denominations (Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican, Anabaptist, etc.). The Catholic Counter‑Reformation (Council of Trent, Jesuits) responded, but the fundamental split between Catholicism and Protestantism persists. | | 3 | **The Old Catholic Schism (19th‑century schism)** | 1870 – 1880 | • The First Vatican Council (1869‑70) defined papal infallibility and the *universal* nature of the papal office.
• A group of bishops and clergy in several European countries (especially the Netherlands, Germany, and Switzerland) rejected these doctrines.
• They formed the Old Catholic Church, maintaining Catholic liturgy and sacramental theology but rejecting papal infallibility and some other doctrines. | Establishment of the Old Catholic Church, which remains in communion with the Union of Utrecht and maintains a distinct identity separate from the Roman Catholic Church. | ### Why these three are singled out 1. **Scale & longevity** – Each schism involved a large portion of Christendom and has had a lasting impact on the structure of the Christian world. 2. **Theological depth** – They each centered on core doctrinal disputes (papal authority, the nature of the Trinity, the role of tradition). 3. **Historical turning points** – They reshaped political alliances, cultural identities, and the spread of Christianity across continents. While other divisions (e.g., the East–West split in the 20th century, the Anglican realignment, or the various schisms within Eastern Orthodoxy) are significant, the three listed above are traditionally regarded as the “greatest” because of their breadth, depth, and enduring legacy.
